content: The findings from the studies can be summarized as follows: 1. Motor Development: One randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted, and no serious limitations were identified. However, there were serious limitations in one study from high-income countries (HICs), and very serious limitations were noted in another study, with no pooled effect size available. The overall quality of evidence was very low. 2. Prosocial Behavior and Socioemotional Development: One RCT was conducted, with no serious limitations identified. However, serious limitations were noted in one study from HICs, and very serious limitations were observed in another study, with no pooled effect size available. The overall quality of evidence was very low. 3. Child Outcomes: Additional findings from five studies showed mixed results. One study reported no effects, one found significant reductions in child behavior problems, and three reported significant reductions in some domains but not all. Ten studies from HICs were included, with overlapping confidence intervals (CIs) in some cases. 4. Caregiver Outcomes: Caregiving Practices: Eight RCTs were conducted. Four studies reported no effects, three showed mixed effects depending on the subscale, and one found significant improvements. Serious limitations were noted in the studies, all of which were from HICs. Caregiver Mental Health: Four RCTs were conducted. Shaw et al. (2008) and Barlow et al. (2015) reported significant declines in mental health issues, while Hiscock et al. (2008, 2018) found no effects. Serious limitations were noted, with all studies conducted in HICs. Caregiving Knowledge: Two RCTs were conducted. Barlow et al. (2015) found significant improvements, while Caldera et al. (2007) reported no effects. Serious limitations were noted, and the data could not be meta-analyzed due to inadequate reporting of means and standard deviations (SDs). 5. Self-Efficacy: Three RCTs were conducted. Breitenstein et al. (2012) and Caldera et al. (2009) found no effects. Serious limitations were noted, and the data could not be meta-analyzed due to missing unadjusted means and SDs. 6. Combined Nutrition and Caregiving Interventions vs. Standard Care: Child Outcomes: Studies showed variation in the magnitude and direction of effects. Some studies reported positive impacts, while others found null or negative effects. Pooled effect sizes often had wide confidence intervals, and many studies had small sample sizes. Language Development: Ten RCTs were conducted. Some studies reported no impacts, while others found positive effects. Pooled results had wide confidence intervals, and three of the six studies had small sample sizes. Socioemotional Development: One RCT found null effects, while others reported positive impacts. Pooled results had wide confidence intervals, and two of the four studies had small sample sizes. 7. Combined Nutrition and Caregiving Interventions vs. Nutrition Interventions: Child Outcomes: Nine studies were included, with five having small sample sizes. Pooled effect sizes had wide confidence intervals, and some studies reported null effects, while others found positive impacts. Language Development: Six RCTs were conducted. Three of the six studies had small sample sizes, and pooled results had wide confidence intervals. Socioemotional Development: One RCT found positive impacts, while others reported null effects. Pooled results had wide confidence intervals, and two of the four studies had small sample sizes. Weight-for-Age Z-Scores (WAZ): Four RCTs were conducted. Two studies had small sample sizes. One study found positive impacts, while others reported no effects. In summary, while some studies demonstrated positive impacts on child and caregiver outcomes, the evidence was often limited by small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, and inconsistent findings across studies. Serious limitations in study design and execution were frequently noted, particularly in studies from HICs.
